claim: Orphans are genes restricted to a single phylogenetic lineage and emerge at high rates.
source: Orphans are genes restricted to a single phylogenetic lineage and emerge at high rates.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: Gene number has remained remarkably constant through evolution despite high rates of orphan emergence.
source: While this predicts an accumulation of genes, the gene number has remained remarkably constant through evolution.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge in the field and citations.

claim: Orphans are not only emerging at a high rate, but they are also rapidly lost.
source: We show that orphans are not only emerging at a high rate, but that they are also rapidly lost.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data presented in figures.

claim: Recently emerged orphans are more likely to be lost than older ones.
source: Interestingly, recently emerged orphans are more likely to be lost than older ones.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10 comparing loss rates across age classes.

claim: Highly expressed orphans with a strong male-bias are more likely to be retained.
source: Furthermore, highly expressed orphans with a strong male-bias are more likely to be retained.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 15, 17, and 18 showing expression and sex-bias patterns.

claim: Both lost and retained orphans show similar evolutionary signatures of functional conservation.
source: Since both lost and retained orphans show similar evolutionary signatures of functional conservation, we propose that orphan loss is not driven by high rates of sequence evolution, but reflects lineage-specific functional requirements.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15 showing similar dN/dS, gene length, and codon usage bias between lost and conserved orphans.

claim: Orphan loss is not driven by high rates of sequence evolution, but reflects lineage-specific functional requirements.
source: Since both lost and retained orphans show similar evolutionary signatures of functional conservation, we propose that orphan loss is not driven by high rates of sequence evolution, but reflects lineage-specific functional requirements.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the data showing similar evolutionary rates between lost and conserved orphans.

claim: Orphans represent a considerable fraction (up to 30%) of the gene catalog in all sequenced genomes.
source: Orphans are genes with limited phylogenetic distribution and represent a considerable fraction (up to 30%) of the gene catalog in all sequenced genomes (Khalturin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Khalturin et al., 2009.

claim: Studies conducted in different eukaryotes showed that orphans emerge at high rates.
source: Studies conducted in different eukaryotes showed that orphans emerge at high rates (Domazet-Loso et al., 2007; Wissler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Domazet-Loso et al., 2007 and Wissler et al., 2013.

claim: Gene duplication and exaptation from transposable elements often result in orphan genes.
source: While gene duplication and exaptation from transposable elements often result in orphan genes (Toll-Riera et al., 2009), they also originate frequently de novo from non-coding DNA (Cai et al., 2008; Heinen et al., 2009; Knowles and McLysaght, 2009; Wu et al., 2011; Yang and Huang, 2011; Xie et al., 2012; Neme and Tautz, 2013; Wu and Zhang, 2013), probably through intermediate proto-genes (Carvunis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Toll-Riera et al., 2009 and other studies.

claim: Orphans also originate frequently de novo from non-coding DNA.
source: While gene duplication and exaptation from transposable elements often result in orphan genes (Toll-Riera et al., 2009), they also originate frequently de novo from non-coding DNA (Cai et al., 2008; Heinen et al., 2009; Knowles and McLysaght, 2009; Wu et al., 2011; Yang and Huang, 2011; Xie et al., 2012; Neme and Tautz, 2013; Wu and Zhang, 2013), probably through intermediate proto-genes (Carvunis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on de novo gene origination.

claim: Orphans probably originate through intermediate proto-genes.
source: While gene duplication and exaptation from transposable elements often result in orphan genes (Toll-Riera et al., 2009), they also originate frequently de novo from non-coding DNA (Cai et al., 2008; Heinen et al., 2009; Knowles and McLysaght, 2009; Wu et al., 2011; Yang and Huang, 2011; Xie et al., 2012; Neme and Tautz, 2013; Wu and Zhang, 2013), probably through intermediate proto-genes (Carvunis et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Carvunis et al., 2012.

claim: Compared to evolutionary conserved genes, orphans are overall shorter.
source: Compared to evolutionary conserved genes, orphans are overall shorter (Lipman et al., 2002), fast evolving (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003), have lower and more tissue-restricted expression (Lemos et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lipman et al., 2002 and confirmed by data in Figure 3A.

claim: Orphans are fast evolving compared to evolutionary conserved genes.
source: Compared to evolutionary conserved genes, orphans are overall shorter (Lipman et al., 2002), fast evolving (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003), have lower and more tissue-restricted expression (Lemos et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003 and confirmed by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Orphans have lower and more tissue-restricted expression compared to evolutionary conserved genes.
source: Compared to evolutionary conserved genes, orphans are overall shorter (Lipman et al., 2002), fast evolving (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003), have lower and more tissue-restricted expression (Lemos et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lemos et al., 2005 and confirmed by data in Figures 3F and 3G.

claim: Orphans often show testis-biased expression.
source: Moreover, they often show testis-biased expression (Levine et al., 2006; Begun et al., 2007), probably due to frequent origination in testis (Kaessmann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levine et al., 2006 and Begun et al., 2007, and confirmed by data in Figure 3H.

claim: Testis-biased expression in orphans is probably due to frequent origination in testis.
source: Moreover, they often show testis-biased expression (Levine et al., 2006; Begun et al., 2007), probably due to frequent origination in testis (Kaessmann, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Kaessmann, 2010.

claim: In Drosophila the rate of orphan emergence is particularly high.
source: In Drosophila the rate of orphan emergence is particulary high (Domazet-Loso et al., 2007) and many orphans become quickly essential (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domazet-Loso et al., 2007.

claim: Many orphans in Drosophila become quickly essential.
source: In Drosophila the rate of orphan emergence is particulary high (Domazet-Loso et al., 2007) and many orphans become quickly essential (Chen et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Orphans might serve an important role in speciation and adaptation to different environments.
source: Although the function of only a few orphan genes has been studied, it has been proposed that orphans might serve an important role in speciation and adaptation to different environments (Khalturin et al., 2008; Khalturin et al., 2009; Colbourne et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a proposed hypothesis supported by citations to Khalturin et al., 2008, 2009 and Colbourne et al., 2011.

claim: The high rate of orphan origination would predict an increase in gene content over time.
source: The high rate of orphan origination would predict an increase in gene content over time.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the observation of high orphan origination rates.

claim: Gene content in eukaryotes is remarkably stable compared to genome size.
source: However, gene content in eukaryotes is remarkably stable compared to genome size, as highlighted by Tautz and Domazet-Loso (2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011.

claim: Tautz and Domazet-Loso proposed that orphans have only a short lifetime ('rapid-turnover' hypothesis).
source: To solve this paradox Tautz and Domazet-Loso proposed that orphans have only a short lifetime ('rapid-turnover' hypothesis) (Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011.

claim: Although orphans are continuously created, most of them might be lost in a relatively short evolutionary time.
source: Thus, although orphans are continuously created, most of them might be lost in a relatively short evolutionary time.
evidence: This is part of the rapid-turnover hypothesis and is supported by the study's findings.

claim: Relaxed selective constraints in orphans might contribute to the high rate of orphan loss.
source: Relaxed selective costraints in orphans (Cai and Petrov, 2010) might also contribute to the high rate of orphan loss.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation supported by a citation to Cai and Petrov, 2010.

claim: Orphans are typically identified by the comparison of distantly related species.
source: Moreover, since orphans are typically identifed by the comparison of distantly related species, their evolutionary stability has been so far neglected.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in previous studies.

claim: The evolutionary stability of orphans has been so far neglected.
source: Moreover, since orphans are typically identifed by the comparison of distantly related species, their evolutionary stability has been so far neglected.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in previous research that this study addresses.

claim: Several partially interrelated factors affect gene loss, including gene expression levels, number of protein–protein interactions, gene dispensability, and rate of sequence evolution.
source: In this study, several partially interrelated factors affect gene loss, including gene expression levels, number of protein–protein interactions, gene dispensability, and rate of sequence evolution (Krylov et al., 2003; Cai and Petrov, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krylov et al., 2003 and Cai and Petrov, 2010.

claim: Orphan age, male-biased gene expression, and microsatellite content are correlated with orphan stability.
source: We investigate the factors contributing to orphan loss and find that orphan age, male-biased gene expression, and microsatellite content are correlated with orphan stability.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data in Figures 10, 15, 17, and 18.

claim: Differences in evolutionary rates cannot explain orphan loss.
source: Surprisingly, differences in evolutionary rates cannot explain orphan loss and we propose that orphan loss is driven by lineage-specific evolutionary constraints.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15C showing similar dN/dS between lost and conserved orphans.

claim: Orphan genes are lost at a significantly higher rate than non-orphan genes.
source: Overall, orphan genes are lost at a significantly higher rate than non-orphan genes, supporting the 'rapid-turnover' hypothesis.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10 showing higher loss rates for orphans compared to old genes.

claim: A BLASTP cutoff of 10−3–10−4 was found to be optimal to maximize sensitivity and specificity in Drosophila.
source: A BLASTP cutoff of 10−3–10−4 was found to be optimal to maximize sensitivity and specificity in Drosophila (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003.

claim: 1152 orphans were identified in D. pseudoobscura, corresponding to 7% of all D. pseudoobscura genes.
source: In total, we identified 1152 orphans, corresponding to 7% of all the D. pseudoobscura genes.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's orphan detection pipeline.

claim: The estimate of 7% orphans in D. pseudoobscura is slightly lower than a previous estimate.
source: Our estimate is slightly lower than a previous one (Zhang et al., 2010), due to our different filtering procedure, but still consistent with a high rate of orphan gain in Drosophila (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003; Domazet-Loso et al., 2007; Zhou et al., 2008; Wissler et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison with a previous study and is supported by citations.

claim: Orphan genes are subject to purifying selection.
source: Our data clearly indicate that orphan genes are subject to purifying selection, as they show several hallmarks of functional protein-coding sequences (Figures 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1 and 2 showing dN/dS < 1, sequence conservation, and codon usage bias.

claim: A comparison of orphan genes preserved between D. pseudoobscura and D. affinis resulted in a distribution of dN/dS significantly lower than 1 with a median of 0.44.
source: A comparison of orphan genes preserved between D. pseudoobscura and D. affinis resulted in a distribution of dN/dS significantly lower than 1 with a median of 0.44 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<1.0 × 10−15), as expected for protein-coding sequences.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: dN/dS for orphans is significantly lower than dN/dS calculated on a random set of intergenic regions with the same length distribution of orphans.
source: Moreover, dN/dS for orphans is significantly lower (Mann–Whitney test, p=2.7 × 10−14) than dN/dS calculated on a random set of intergenic regions with the same length distribution of orphans (see 'Materials and methods', section 'Evolutionary rates') (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study supported by Figure 1A.

claim: Orphans are more conserved than intergenic regions.
source: Consistent with this, we also found orphans to be more conserved than intergenic regions (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The codon usage bias of orphans is intermediate to that of old genes and intergenic regions.
source: The codon usage bias of orphans is intermediate to that of old genes and intergenic regions (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1C.

claim: pN/pS for orphans is significantly lower compared to intergenic regions.
source: We found that pN/pS for orphans is significantly lower compared to intergenic regions (Mann–Whitney test, p=0.02182) (Figure 2), and significantly greater for old genes (Mann–Whitney test, p<1.0 × 10−15), consistent with purifying selection operating on orphans.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study supported by Figure 2.

claim: pN/pS for orphans is significantly greater than for old genes.
source: We found that pN/pS for orphans is significantly lower compared to intergenic regions (Mann–Whitney test, p=0.02182) (Figure 2), and significantly greater for old genes (Mann–Whitney test, p<1.0 × 10−15), consistent with purifying selection operating on orphans.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study supported by Figure 2.

claim: Orphan genes are shorter than old genes (median length for orphans = 344 bp, median length for old genes = 1470 bp).
source: In agreement with studies in other species (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003; Toll-Riera et al., 2009; Wolf et al., 2009; Cai and Petrov, 2010; Capra et al., 2010; Carvunis et al., 2012), we also find that orphan genes are shorter (median length for orphans = 344 bp, median length for old genes = 1470 bp), have a lower GC content (median GC content for orphans = 0.54, median GC content for old genes = 0.55), are expressed at lower levels (expression in D. pseudoobscura males: mean expression for orphans = 29 FPKM, mean expression for old genes = 41 FPKM) than old genes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A and citations to previous studies.

claim: Orphans have a lower GC content than old genes (median GC content for orphans = 0.54, median GC content for old genes = 0.55).
source: In agreement with studies in other species (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003; Toll-Riera et al., 2009; Wolf et al., 2009; Cai and Petrov, 2010; Capra et al., 2010; Carvunis et al., 2012), we also find that orphan genes are shorter (median length for orphans = 344 bp, median length for old genes = 1470 bp), have a lower GC content (median GC content for orphans = 0.54, median GC content for old genes = 0.55), are expressed at lower levels (expression in D. pseudoobscura males: mean expression for orphans = 29 FPKM, mean expression for old genes = 41 FPKM) than old genes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3B and citations to previous studies.

claim: Orphans are expressed at lower levels than old genes (expression in D. pseudoobscura males: mean expression for orphans = 29 FPKM, mean expression for old genes = 41 FPKM).
source: In agreement with studies in other species (Domazet-Loso and Tautz, 2003; Toll-Riera et al., 2009; Wolf et al., 2009; Cai and Petrov, 2010; Capra et al., 2010; Carvunis et al., 2012), we also find that orphan genes are shorter (median length for orphans = 344 bp, median length for old genes = 1470 bp), have a lower GC content (median GC content for orphans = 0.54, median GC content for old genes = 0.55), are expressed at lower levels (expression in D. pseudoobscura males: mean expression for orphans = 29 FPKM, mean expression for old genes = 41 FPKM) than old genes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3F and citations to previous studies.

claim: The fraction of genes with a paralog (>90% protein similarity) is similar for orphans (6.9%) and old genes (6.4%).
source: Using CD-Hit (Li and Godzik, 2006), we found the fraction of genes with a paralog (>90% protein similarity) to be similar for orphans (6.9%) and old genes (6.4%).
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's analysis using CD-Hit.

claim: Orphans are more enriched in microsatellites than old genes.
source: Orphans are more enriched in microsatellites, also consistent with previous findings in vertebrates (Toll-Riera et al., 2012) and rice (Guo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3D and citations to previous studies.

claim: Unlike mammals, none of the D. pseudoobscura orphans was found to be associated with transposable elements.
source: Furthermore, unlike mammals (Toll-Riera et al., 2009), none of the D. pseudoobscura orphans was found to be associated with transposable elements (see 'Transposons detection').
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's transposon detection analysis.

claim: The distribution of orphans is heterogeneous across chromosomes.
source: The distribution of orphans is heterogeneous across chromosomes (χ2-test, p<1.0 × 10−15), with the X chromosome having the highest fraction of orphans.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: The X chromosome has the highest fraction of orphans.
source: The distribution of orphans is heterogeneous across chromosomes (χ2-test, p<1.0 × 10−15), with the X chromosome having the highest fraction of orphans.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: In the obscura group, the two X-chromosome arms have a different evolutionary history.
source: In the obscura group, the two X-chromosome arms have a different evolutionary history. XL corresponds to Muller's element A and is homologous to the X chromosome in D. melanogaster. XR, however, has been recently derived from an autosome (Muller's element D, 3L in D. melanogaster).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary history of the obscura group.

claim: XL corresponds to Muller's element A and is homologous to the X chromosome in D. melanogaster.
source: In the obscura group, the two X-chromosome arms have a different evolutionary history. XL corresponds to Muller's element A and is homologous to the X chromosome in D. melanogaster. XR, however, has been recently derived from an autosome (Muller's element D, 3L in D. melanogaster).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary history of the obscura group.

claim: XR has been recently derived from an autosome (Muller's element D, 3L in D. melanogaster).
source: In the obscura group, the two X-chromosome arms have a different evolutionary history. XL corresponds to Muller's element A and is homologous to the X chromosome in D. melanogaster. XR, however, has been recently derived from an autosome (Muller's element D, 3L in D. melanogaster).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the evolutionary history of the obscura group.

claim: The old-X is responsible for the excess of X-linked orphan genes.
source: Analyzing the old-X and neo-X chromosomes separately, we observed a striking difference in the number of orphans despite similar chromosome sizes, with the old-X responsible for the excess of X-linked orphan genes, and the neo-X showing a similar number of orphans as the autosomes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: The neo-X shows a similar number of orphans as the autosomes.
source: Analyzing the old-X and neo-X chromosomes separately, we observed a striking difference in the number of orphans despite similar chromosome sizes, with the old-X responsible for the excess of X-linked orphan genes, and the neo-X showing a similar number of orphans as the autosomes (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4.

claim: Average GC content, microsatellite density, transposon density, and length of intergenic regions differ between the old-X and neo-X chromosomal arms.
source: For each chromosomal arm, we computed genomic features in 100 kb windows to correlate them with the difference in orphan content between old-X and neo-X. We found that average GC content, microsatellite density, transposon density, and length of intergenic regions differ between the two chromosomal arms (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5.

claim: The difference in orphan number between old-X and neo-X chromosomes should date back to the time before the origin of the neo-X, with a similar number of orphans originating after the creation of the neo-X, if orphan genes emerge at a higher rate on the X-chromosome.
source: If orphan genes emerge at a higher rate on the X-chromosome (Levine et al., 2006), the shorter history of X-linkage on the neo-X could explain the paucity of orphans on the neo-X compared to old-X. In this case, the difference in orphan number between old-X and neo-X chromosomes should date back to the time before the origin of the neo-X, with a similar number of orphans originating after the creation of the neo-X.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested by the study.

claim: A consistent paucity of orphans on XR relative to XL was observed across all age classes.
source: Surprisingly, we observed a consistent paucity of orphans on XR relative to XL across all age classes (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 7.

claim: X-linkage is not sufficient to explain the enrichment of orphans on XL.
source: This persistent difference in orphan number between XL and XR in all age classes suggests that X-linkage is not sufficient to explain the enrichment of orphans on XL.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data in Figure 7.

claim: The former autosome differs from the ancestral X chromosomal arm by a yet unidentified feature that affects the emergence of new orphans.
source: We conclude that the former autosome differs from the ancestral X chromosomal arm by a yet unidentified feature that affects the emergence of new orphans.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing persistent differences in orphan numbers.

claim: The oldest orphans (age class 4) show a pronounced excess of pseudogenized orphans on XR in D. affinis and D. miranda.
source: The analysis of orphans that have putatively lost their function via the acquisition of a stop codon or a frame shift causing insertion/deletion (pseudogenized/lost orphans) reveals another interesting feature of the XL–XR fusion. The oldest orphans in our dataset (age class 4) show a pronounced excess of pseudogenized orphans on XR in D. affinis and D. miranda (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: The trend of excess pseudogenized orphans on XR was not observed for orphans that emerged on XR after the XL–XR fusion.
source: This trend was not observed for orphans that emerged on XR after the XL–XR fusion (Figure 8B,C), nor for old genes (Figure 8D) and is not due to an increased rate of orphan gain on XR (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 8B, 8C, 8D, and 9.

claim: The high rate of pseudogenization of orphans on the XR may reflect the new X-linkage of previously autosomal orphans.
source: Since the oldest orphans (age class 4) on XR are a mixture of autosomal (i.e., before the fusion) and sex-chromosomal (i.e., after the fusion) orphans, we speculate that the high rate of pseudogenization of orphans on the XR may reflect the new X-linkage of previously autosomal orphans.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation based on the data.

claim: The XR chromosome has experienced a burst of gene duplications to autosomes after its creation.
source: A previous study (Meisel et al., 2009) found that the XR chromosome has experienced a burst of gene duplications to autosomes after its creation.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Meisel et al., 2009.

claim: Only 1 out of 21 genes in D. miranda and 1 out of 14 genes in D. lowei had a second hit on an autosome covering at least 50% of the length of the query gene.
source: Upon manual inspection of the alignments, we found that only 1 out of 21 genes in D. miranda (gene ID: GA23486) and 1 out of 14 genes in D. lowei (gene ID: GA23807) had a second hit on an autosome covering at least 50% of the length of the query gene.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's analysis of gene duplications.

claim: Duplication of orphans cannot explain the excess of pseudogenized orphans on XR.
source: Thus, we conclude that duplication of orphans cannot explain the excess of pseudogenized orphans on XR.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of gene duplications.

claim: The emergence of the neo-X chromosome influenced the orphan dynamics on XR, affecting rates of both gain and loss.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis clearly indicates that the emergence of the neo-X chromosome influenced the orphan dynamics on XR, affecting rates of both gain and loss, thus we excluded this chromosome arm for our analyses of the rate of orphan turnover.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing differential orphan dynamics on XR.

claim: The fraction of orphan pseudogenes decreases with age.
source: In the D. persimilis lineage, orphan pseudogenization can be studied for three different age classes. If orphans of all age classes were functionally equivalent, no difference in the rate of orphan pseudogenization would be expected. We observe, however, that the fraction of orphan pseudogenes decreases with age (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: The D. miranda lineage also shows a higher loss of young orphan genes.
source: The D. miranda lineage also shows a higher loss of young orphan genes. The relatively small number of observations, however, precludes statistical testing of this trend.
evidence: This is an observation from the data, but statistical testing is not possible due to small sample size.

claim: Orphan genes are lost significantly more often than old genes.
source: Overall, orphan genes are lost significantly more often than old genes (Fisher's exact test, p=3.3 × 10−8), consistent with the rapid turnover hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: PTCs are enriched at the beginning and at the end of the ORF.
source: When looking at the distribution of premature termination codons (PTC) along the open reading frame (ORF) of all genes, we observed that PTCs are enriched at the beginning and at the end of the ORF (Figure 12), consistent with previous results in D. melanogaster (Lee and Reinhardt, 2012) and D. pseudoobscura (Hoehn et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 12 and citations to previous studies.

claim: Orphans of age class 3 are lost more often than those of age class 4 when considering only ORF-disrupting mutations localized in the first half of the ORF.
source: Since ORF-disrupting mutations occuring at the end of the ORF might have little impact on gene function, we redefined pseudogenes by considering only ORF-disrupting mutations localized in the first half of the ORF and confirmed that orphans of age class 3 are lost more often than those of age class 4 (Figure 13).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 13.

claim: Conserved orphans have a higher GC content than lost orphans.
source: Conserved orphans have a higher GC content, contain fewer microsatellites, are expressed at a higher level and are more male-biased (Figure 15B,D–F,G,H) compared to lost orphans.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15B.

claim: Conserved orphans contain fewer microsatellites than lost orphans.
source: Conserved orphans have a higher GC content, contain fewer microsatellites, are expressed at a higher level and are more male-biased (Figure 15B,D–F,G,H) compared to lost orphans.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15D.

claim: Conserved orphans are expressed at a higher level than lost orphans.
source: Conserved orphans have a higher GC content, contain fewer microsatellites, are expressed at a higher level and are more male-biased (Figure 15B,D–F,G,H) compared to lost orphans.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 15F and 15G.

claim: Conserved orphans are more male-biased than lost orphans.
source: Conserved orphans have a higher GC content, contain fewer microsatellites, are expressed at a higher level and are more male-biased (Figure 15B,D–F,G,H) compared to lost orphans.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15H.

claim: Conserved orphans tend to increase their expression level as they become older.
source: Conserved orphans tend to increase their expression level as they become older (Figure 16A), whereas the opposite pattern is true for lost orphans (Figure 16B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 16A.

claim: Lost orphans tend to decrease their expression level as they become older.
source: Conserved orphans tend to increase their expression level as they become older (Figure 16A), whereas the opposite pattern is true for lost orphans (Figure 16B).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 16B.

claim: Orphan genes are frequently expressed in the testis.
source: Orphan genes are frequently expressed in the testis (Levine et al., 2006; Begun et al., 2007) and have a male-biased gene expression pattern (Metta and Schlötterer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levine et al., 2006, Begun et al., 2007, and Metta and Schlötterer, 2008.

claim: Orphan genes have a male-biased gene expression pattern.
source: Orphan genes are frequently expressed in the testis (Levine et al., 2006; Begun et al., 2007) and have a male-biased gene expression pattern (Metta and Schlötterer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Metta and Schlötterer, 2008 and data in Figure 3H.

claim: Pervasive gene expression in testis facilitates the functional recruitment of non-specific expression.
source: This pattern could be generated by pervasive gene expression in testis, which facilitates the functional recruitment of non-specific expression (Kaessmann, 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by a citation to Kaessmann, 2010.

claim: Expression in testis does not require a complex architecture of regulatory modules.
source: Another explanation is that expression in testis does not require a complex architecture of regulatory modules (Sassone-Corsi, 2002; Kleene, 2005; Kaessmann, 2010), so that fewer substitutions are required to obtain a functional regulatory module for expressing a novel gene in testis compared to other tissues.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Sassone-Corsi, 2002, Kleene, 2005, and Kaessmann, 2010.

claim: The fraction of male-biased genes increases with the age of the orphan genes.
source: Unexpectedly, the fraction of male-biased genes increases with the age of the orphan genes (Figure 17).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 17.

claim: The increase of male-biased orphans among the older age classes is the result of a preferential loss of orphans with an unbiased gene expression.
source: This increase of male-biased orphans among the older age classes is the result of a preferential loss of orphans with an unbiased gene expression (Figure 18).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 18.

claim: Lost orphans have a significantly lower male-bias in D. miranda.
source: Consistent with the gene expression pattern in D. pseudoobscura, we found that lost orphans have a significantly lower male-bias in D. miranda (Figure 19).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 19.

claim: The previously reported male-biased gene expression of orphan genes is not the result of a preferential recruitment of male-biased transcripts.
source: We conclude that the previously reported male-biased gene expression of orphan genes is not the result of a preferential recruitment of male-biased transcripts, nor do orphans gradually acquire male-biased gene expression. Rather, male-biased orphans are more likely to be retained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing preferential retention of male-biased orphans.

claim: Orphans do not gradually acquire male-biased gene expression.
source: We conclude that the previously reported male-biased gene expression of orphan genes is not the result of a preferential recruitment of male-biased transcripts, nor do orphans gradually acquire male-biased gene expression. Rather, male-biased orphans are more likely to be retained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data showing preferential retention of male-biased orphans.

claim: Male-biased orphans are more likely to be retained.
source: We conclude that the previously reported male-biased gene expression of orphan genes is not the result of a preferential recruitment of male-biased transcripts, nor do orphans gradually acquire male-biased gene expression. Rather, male-biased orphans are more likely to be retained.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data in Figures 17, 18, and 19.

claim: Until now, orphan evolution was primarily studied on long phylogenetic branches.
source: Until now, orphan evolution was primarily studied on long phylogenetic branches.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of previous research.

claim: Studying orphan evolution on long phylogenetic branches is well suited to discover new orphans, but does not allow tracing the evolution of orphans.
source: Although this approach is well suited to discover new orphans, it does not allow tracing the evolution of orphans.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of previous approaches.

claim: Previous studies showed a high rate of orphan gain, which is not reflected in an increase in gene number.
source: Previous studies showed a high rate of orphan gain, which is not reflected in an increase in gene number.
evidence: This is a summary of previous findings.

claim: It has been postulated that orphans must be lost at a high rate as well to resolve the paradox of high orphan gain without increase in gene number.
source: To resolve this apparent paradox, it has been postulated that orphans must be lost at a high rate as well (Tautz and Domazet-Loso, 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work that this study tests.

claim: Most losses (~76%) were due to disabling mutations rather than deletions of the orphan gene.
source: Interestingly, most losses (∼76%) were due to disabling mutations rather than deletions of the orphan gene.
evidence: This is a direct result from the study's analysis of orphan losses.

claim: Under equilibrium conditions the number of losses balances the number of orphan gains.
source: Although under equilibrium conditions the number of losses balances the number of orphan gains, here, we observed a surplus of orphan gains (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a theoretical expectation that is not met in the data.

claim: A surplus of orphan gains was observed in this study.
source: Although under equilibrium conditions the number of losses balances the number of orphan gains, here, we observed a surplus of orphan gains (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6.

claim: The discrepancy between orphan gains and losses probably does not imply an increase of gene number, but rather reflects the limited evolutionary time to acquire mutations.
source: We caution that this discrepancy probably does not imply an increase of gene number, but rather reflects the limited evolutionary time to acquire mutations.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed surplus of orphan gains.

claim: Using a rather conservative criterion for disabling mutations, either premature stop codons or frameshift indels, we have probably not identified all orphans that have lost their function.
source: Using a rather conservative criterion for disabling mutations, either premature stop codons or frameshift indels, we have probably not identified all orphans that have lost their function.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's methodology.

claim: The study does not account for the possibility of loss of function due to changes in gene regulation.
source: Furthermore, we do not account for the possibility of loss of function due to changes in gene regulation.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of the study's methodology.

claim: Codon usage bias, dN/dS values and sequence conservation clearly suggest that orphan genes are functionally constrained.
source: Importantly, codon usage bias, dN/dS values and sequence conservation clearly suggest that orphan genes are functionally constrained and these constraints do not differ among orphans that are conserved in the obscura group and those that lost function in at least one species of the group.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 1, 2, and 15.

claim: Functional constraints on orphans do not differ among orphans that are conserved in the obscura group and those that lost function in at least one species of the group.
source: Importantly, codon usage bias, dN/dS values and sequence conservation clearly suggest that orphan genes are functionally constrained and these constraints do not differ among orphans that are conserved in the obscura group and those that lost function in at least one species of the group.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15 showing similar evolutionary rates between lost and conserved orphans.

claim: It may be possible that orphan loss is stochastic and reflects weak purifying selection.
source: Hence, it may be possible that orphan loss is stochastic and reflects weak purifying selection.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claim: Lost orphans differ in some aspects from conserved ones: orphans that are lost contain more microsatellite stretches and have a lower, less sex-biased gene expression than retained ones.
source: Nevertheless, lost orphans differ in some aspects from conserved ones. Orphans that are lost contain more microsatellite stretches and have a lower, less sex-biased gene expression than retained ones.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 15.

claim: The rate of orphan loss decreases with orphan age.
source: Furthermore, we also found that the rate of orphan loss decreases with orphan age, a result consistent with orphans serving a functional role only temporarily.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 10.

claim: The result that the rate of orphan loss decreases with orphan age is consistent with orphans serving a functional role only temporarily.
source: Furthermore, we also found that the rate of orphan loss decreases with orphan age, a result consistent with orphans serving a functional role only temporarily.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on age-dependent orphan loss.

claim: Previous work suggested that orphans are important for adaptation to novel environments.
source: Previous work suggested that orphans are important for adaptation to novel environments (Khalturin et al., 2009; Colbourne et al., 2011), but it is also possible that orphans contribute to stabilize new connections in gene networks (Capra et al., 2010; Warnefors and Eyre-Walker, 2011) and become obsolete once such new connections have been optimized.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work supported by citations.

claim: It is also possible that orphans contribute to stabilize new connections in gene networks and become obsolete once such new connections have been optimized.
source: Previous work suggested that orphans are important for adaptation to novel environments (Khalturin et al., 2009; Colbourne et al., 2011), but it is also possible that orphans contribute to stabilize new connections in gene networks (Capra et al., 2010; Warnefors and Eyre-Walker, 2011) and become obsolete once such new connections have been optimized.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Capra et al., 2010 and Warnefors and Eyre-Walker, 2011.

claim: Orphans become quickly functional, which is reflected in their codon usage bias, dN/dS ratio and sequence conservation.
source: Our data suggest that orphans become quickly functional, which is reflected in their codon usage bias, dN/dS ratio and sequence conservation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: The neo-X is now fully dosage compensated.
source: Despite the fact that the neo-X is now fully dosage compensated (Abraham and Lucchesi, 1974), and has obtained a similar base composition as the XL (Gallach et al., 2007), we noted that the translocation resulted in a preferential loss of orphan genes on the neo-X.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Abraham and Lucchesi, 1974.

claim: The neo-X has obtained a similar base composition as the XL.
source: Despite the fact that the neo-X is now fully dosage compensated (Abraham and Lucchesi, 1974), and has obtained a similar base composition as the XL (Gallach et al., 2007), we noted that the translocation resulted in a preferential loss of orphan genes on the neo-X.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Gallach et al., 2007.

claim: The translocation resulted in a preferential loss of orphan genes on the neo-X.
source: Despite the fact that the neo-X is now fully dosage compensated (Abraham and Lucchesi, 1974), and has obtained a similar base composition as the XL (Gallach et al., 2007), we noted that the translocation resulted in a preferential loss of orphan genes on the neo-X.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8A.

claim: The pattern of preferential loss of orphan genes on the neo-X is restricted to orphans that most likely originated before the chromosomal fusion.
source: Since this pattern is restricted to orphans that most likely originated before the chromosomal fusion, we argue that the change in chromosomal environment has affected the function of orphan genes, most likely via expression differences.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 8.

claim: The change in chromosomal environment has affected the function of orphan genes, most likely via expression differences.
source: Since this pattern is restricted to orphans that most likely originated before the chromosomal fusion, we argue that the change in chromosomal environment has affected the function of orphan genes, most likely via expression differences.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data on preferential loss of orphans on the neo-X.

claim: The selective advantage conferred by these orphans has diminished, which resulted in a higher loss rate.
source: We speculate that the selective advantage conferred by these orphans has diminished, which resulted in a higher loss rate.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the higher loss rate of orphans on the neo-X.

claim: The elevated rate of orphan loss after the neo-X formation seems to be still ongoing.
source: Interestingly, the elevated rate of orphan loss after the neo-X formation seems to be still ongoing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing continued differential loss rates.

claim: The differential loss of orphan genes point in a similar direction as the observation that the gene composition of the neo-X has been altered by gene duplication.
source: This differential loss of orphan genes point in a similar direction as the observation that the gene composition of the neo-X has been altered by gene duplication (Meisel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation connecting the study's findings with previous work.

claim: Both (orphan) gene loss and duplication contribute to fast gene content remodeling on a newly formed sex chromosome in Drosophila.
source: Hence, both (orphan) gene loss and duplication contribute to fast gene content remodeling on a newly formed sex chromosome in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings and previous work on gene duplication.
